items.title: Michael Burry says the best defense against dollar doom and AI disasters might be a fine Bordeaux
items.summary: Michael Burry of "The Big Short" sees fine wines as a compelling investment. Bloomberg/Getty Images Michael Burry made the case for investing in fine wines in a Substack post on Thursday. The "Big Short" investor said they're a "terrific diversifier" for portfolios. Burry said fine wines could benefit from dollar decline, fiat flight, and AI fallout. Michael Burry has turned from water to wine. The star of "The Big Short," who made waves for investing in water after calling the collapse of the mid-2000s US housing bubble, explained why he's betting on fine wines in a Substack post on Thursday. Burry, who pivoted from running a hedge fund to writing about his personal investments almost a year ago, told his subscribers that fine wines could be a "terrific diversifier" for their portfolios. He wrote that "just about every single case of fine wine sitting in a London bonded warehouse can be a short position on the US dollar, a global hedge against fiat currency, and a ward against global financial systems' vulnerability to the various hellscapes possibly wrought by future iterations of AI and quantum computing." Burry said that if new technologies threaten the digital financial system, the greenback "could accelerate its ongoing loss of reserve status to real assets." One beneficiary could be fine wines, as the Liv-ex Fine Wine 100 index has been negatively correlated to the US Dollar Index across overlapping five-year periods, he said. Burry said fine wines could function as a hedge against the "colossal train wreck" he expects for the dollar over the next five to 10 years, as the "bills of fiscal irresponsibility come due." He was referring to the US national debt, which has roughly doubled since 2010 to a record $40 trillion , and the government's interest payments, which account for more than $1 trillion of its roughly $7 trillion annual budget. Making the case Burry described how fine wines are highly differentiated and have a set drinking window, so "every bottle of wine consumed anywhere on earth shrinks the inventory of that exact asset forever." "Supply destruction is both continuous and a bullish supply dynamic that spirits, watches, and art can never match," he added. Burry pointed out that the finest wines — including Pétrus, Margaux, and Mouton Rothschild — cater to the ultra-wealthy, so they "inspire resilient demand in good and bad times." However, their hefty price tags likely restrict this trade to investors who can afford to spend five figures on wines and have them only account for 10% or less of their portfolios, he said. When I ran money, investors wound ask me to share with them any alternative investments I like or can get behind. Now, I can share them with you. They do not come along often. https://t.co/R8ZBhg1xsB — Cassandra Unchained (@michaeljburry) September 11, 2026 Burry, a value investor, said a key reason to buy into fine wines now is that prices have tumbled by around 25% to 30% from their October 2022 peak. He also emphasized the appeal of gaining easy access to exceptional wines to drink and gift to others. Moreover, he underlined the " sturdy value of bonded fine wine as we face what could be a technological paradigm shift for the ages alongside a decline in the dollar's status as a reserve currency." Burry cited a study that found fine wines delivered an annual net real return of 4.1% between 1900 and 2012. He said that investors today stand to make four or five times their money over the next 20 years, as they're buying into a depressed market and could profit from a weakening dollar. He also found that European fine wines show virtually no correlation to the S&P 500 over the last 25 years, making them a "near-perfect diversifier " that performs similarly to the US stock market over time. However, he urged readers to " wait for the best wines at the best prices," noting that he considered around 700 wines this year but only bought around 40. Burry said fine wines, along with other real assets such as gold and real estate, appeal to him "given the future we face, both financially and technologically." Read the original article on Business Insider
items.summary_html:
Michael Burry of "The Big Short" sees fine wines as a compelling investment.

Bloomberg/Getty Images

  • Michael Burry made the case for investing in fine wines in a Substack post on Thursday.
  • The "Big Short" investor said they're a "terrific diversifier" for portfolios.
  • Burry said fine wines could benefit from dollar decline, fiat flight, and AI fallout.

Michael Burry has turned from water to wine.

The star of "The Big Short," who made waves for investing in water after calling the collapse of the mid-2000s US housing bubble, explained why he's betting on fine wines in a Substack post on Thursday.

Burry, who pivoted from running a hedge fund to writing about his personal investments almost a year ago, told his subscribers that fine wines could be a "terrific diversifier" for their portfolios.

He wrote that "just about every single case of fine wine sitting in a London bonded warehouse can be a short position on the US dollar, a global hedge against fiat currency, and a ward against global financial systems' vulnerability to the various hellscapes possibly wrought by future iterations of AI and quantum computing."

Burry said that if new technologies threaten the digital financial system, the greenback "could accelerate its ongoing loss of reserve status to real assets."

One beneficiary could be fine wines, as the Liv-ex Fine Wine 100 index has been negatively correlated to the US Dollar Index across overlapping five-year periods, he said.

Burry said fine wines could function as a hedge against the "colossal train wreck" he expects for the dollar over the next five to 10 years, as the "bills of fiscal irresponsibility come due."

He was referring to the US national debt, which has roughly doubled since 2010 to a record $40 trillion, and the government's interest payments, which account for more than $1 trillion of its roughly $7 trillion annual budget.

Making the case

Burry described how fine wines are highly differentiated and have a set drinking window, so "every bottle of wine consumed anywhere on earth shrinks the inventory of that exact asset forever."

"Supply destruction is both continuous and a bullish supply dynamic that spirits, watches, and art can never match," he added.

Burry pointed out that the finest wines — including Pétrus, Margaux, and Mouton Rothschild — cater to the ultra-wealthy, so they "inspire resilient demand in good and bad times."

However, their hefty price tags likely restrict this trade to investors who can afford to spend five figures on wines and have them only account for 10% or less of their portfolios, he said.

When I ran money, investors wound ask me to share with them any alternative investments I like or can get behind. Now, I can share them with you.

They do not come along often. https://t.co/R8ZBhg1xsB

— Cassandra Unchained (@michaeljburry) September 11, 2026

Burry, a value investor, said a key reason to buy into fine wines now is that prices have tumbled by around 25% to 30% from their October 2022 peak.

He also emphasized the appeal of gaining easy access to exceptional wines to drink and gift to others.

Moreover, he underlined the "sturdy value of bonded fine wine as we face what could be a technological paradigm shift for the ages alongside a decline in the dollar's status as a reserve currency."

Burry cited a study that found fine wines delivered an annual net real return of 4.1% between 1900 and 2012. He said that investors today stand to make four or five times their money over the next 20 years, as they're buying into a depressed market and could profit from a weakening dollar.

He also found that European fine wines show virtually no correlation to the S&P 500 over the last 25 years, making them a "near-perfect diversifier" that performs similarly to the US stock market over time.

However, he urged readers to "wait for the best wines at the best prices," noting that he considered around 700 wines this year but only bought around 40.

Burry said fine wines, along with other real assets such as gold and real estate, appeal to him "given the future we face, both financially and technologically."

items.title: Soft-deprecating re.match()
items.summary: Soft-deprecating re.match() Python has a concept of soft deprecation , where APIs are marked as "should no longer be used to write new code" without any promise/threat to remove them in the future. Python 3.15 release manager Hugo van Kemenade describes how in the upcoming 3.15 release soft deprecation has come for the venerable but deeply confusing re.match() function. It's now available with the much clearer alternative re.prefixmatch() name - reflecting how it anchors at the beginning of the string but not the end. Most of the time you probably want re.search() (match this pattern anywhere in the string) or re.fullmatch() (match the entire string) instead. Via Lobste.rs Tags: python , regular-expressions
items.summary_html:
Soft-deprecating re.match()

Python has a concept of soft deprecation, where APIs are marked as "should no longer be used to write new code" without any promise/threat to remove them in the future.

Python 3.15 release manager Hugo van Kemenade describes how in the upcoming 3.15 release soft deprecation has come for the venerable but deeply confusing re.match() function. It's now available with the much clearer alternative re.prefixmatch() name - reflecting how it anchors at the beginning of the string but not the end.

Most of the time you probably want re.search() (match this pattern anywhere in the string) or re.fullmatch() (match the entire string) instead.

Via Lobste.rs

Tags: python, regular-expressions

items.title: Don't sleep on wrapture
items.summary: Graham Dumpleton's new monkey patching package wrapture is shaping up to be an indispensable tool for Python developers. I'm not sure why I've seen so little buzz about it! Graham has been posting new tutorials for it almost daily since the initial release on August 31st. Here's everything he's published so far: Introducing wrapture - a new monkey patching library that serves both testing and observability (think New Relic style tracing) at the same time. Unit testing with wrapture - how to use it for the same kinds of thing as unittest.mock . Recording calls with wrapture - recording method calls as timelines and processing and displaying them as trees. Phased behaviour in wrapture - arranging patched methods to change behavior across multiple calls. Beyond callables in wrapture - monkey patching attributes, dictionaries, generators. Live tracing with wrapture - tracing a live application to see exactly how it works. Zero-code tracing with wrapture - configuring tracing in a separate TOML file without modifying Python code at all. Tracing Flask with wrapture - using the separate wrapture-instrumenation package to instrument a Flask application. That package also provides instrumentation for aiohttp.client , aiohttp.web , django , fastapi , flask , grpc , http.client , httpx , jinja2 , requests , sqlalchemy , sqlite3 , starlette , urllib.request , urllib3 , uvicorn , werkzeug.serving , wsgiref.simple_server , xmlrpc.client , xmlrpc.server . Finding slow code with wrapture - wrapture's tools for recording timing information, both individually and aggregated across multiple calls. OpenTelemetry export in wrapture - exporting traces to OpenTelemetry. Graham also has a set of interactive workshops for wrapture, implemented as JupyterLab notebooks. Wrapture is still alpha software but it's already very usable - especially given you can configure and try it out with a TOML file without modifying any Python code at all. This feels like one of those Swiss Army Knife packages that, once mastered, will provide value against all sorts of problems for years to come. Tags: graham-dumpleton , open-source , testing , python , observability , monkey-patching
items.summary_html:
Graham Dumpleton's new monkey patching package wrapture is shaping up to be an indispensable tool for Python developers. I'm not sure why I've seen so little buzz about it!

Graham has been posting new tutorials for it almost daily since the initial release on August 31st. Here's everything he's published so far:

  • Introducing wrapture - a new monkey patching library that serves both testing and observability (think New Relic style tracing) at the same time.
  • Unit testing with wrapture - how to use it for the same kinds of thing as unittest.mock.
  • Recording calls with wrapture - recording method calls as timelines and processing and displaying them as trees.
  • Phased behaviour in wrapture - arranging patched methods to change behavior across multiple calls.
  • Beyond callables in wrapture - monkey patching attributes, dictionaries, generators.
  • Live tracing with wrapture - tracing a live application to see exactly how it works.
  • Zero-code tracing with wrapture - configuring tracing in a separate TOML file without modifying Python code at all.
  • Tracing Flask with wrapture - using the separate wrapture-instrumenation package to instrument a Flask application. That package also provides instrumentation for aiohttp.client, aiohttp.web, django, fastapi, flask, grpc, http.client, httpx, jinja2, requests, sqlalchemy, sqlite3, starlette, urllib.request, urllib3, uvicorn, werkzeug.serving, wsgiref.simple_server, xmlrpc.client, xmlrpc.server.
  • Finding slow code with wrapture - wrapture's tools for recording timing information, both individually and aggregated across multiple calls.
  • OpenTelemetry export in wrapture - exporting traces to OpenTelemetry.

Graham also has a set of interactive workshops for wrapture, implemented as JupyterLab notebooks.

Wrapture is still alpha software but it's already very usable - especially given you can configure and try it out with a TOML file without modifying any Python code at all.

This feels like one of those Swiss Army Knife packages that, once mastered, will provide value against all sorts of problems for years to come.

items.title: ‘We Did Not Invite You.’ Citizens Rage at Town Hall Over Proposed Nuclear AI Data Center
items.summary: Representatives from the University of Michigan faced tough questions and a lot of vitriol from the citizens of Ypsilanti Township Wednesday night. The University partnered with America’s nuclear weapons scientists at Los Alamos National Laboratories (LANL) to build a hyperscale data center in the Township and residents are pissed . On Wednesday night the University hosted a town hall meant to ameliorate people’s anger and concerns. It didn’t work. LANL and U of M want to build a $1.2 billion 220,000 hyperscale data center in Ypsilanti Township. The residents are worried about electricity costs, water usage, and noise like other communities across the country considering data centers. But citizens and leaders of the Township are also worried that this particular data center would further nuclear weapon research. They’ve also said the University has condescended to them during the entire process, lied, and ignored them. Judging by footage of the Wednesday night’s town hall , U of M didn’t win anyone over and openly deepened citizens’ anger and mistrust. U of M faculty director Patricia Hurn delivered a prepared statement while people in the audience shouted at her. “This facility is going to be used for many different purposes including improving cancer care, strengthening the power grid, accelerating drug discovery, and sustainable computing,” she said over jeers from the crowd. “Many of us are interested in finding the generalized cure for cancer,” Hurn said. The crowd laughed and mocked her. She pressed on. “And many of us want to drop infant mortality. Some of us want clean energy. “How about healthcare?” Someone shouted from the crowd. “All of those things are going to require — and some of you are listening to me so I’ll just keep talking to you — some of us want those answers and we know that to get them is going to take really strong and big abilities to do computing,” she said. Steven Ceccio, the project’s lead engineer, attempted to address some of the practical concerns surrounding the project. “The project is tremendously smaller in scope and size than these commercial data centers,” he said, pointing to a slide that compared the size of the proposed LANL data center to The Barn in nearby Saline Township , a massive $56 billion 1.4 gigawatt OpenAI project. Later in the night, a man named Andy called Ceccio out. He said he worked in data centers all around the country. “I think it’s convenient that this is 1/20th the size of a data center when you’re comparing it to The Barn that’s going over in Saline. That’s an aberration. That’s not a normal sized data center. When you compare the data center that you’re about to build to the average data center in the United States, you’re at the very top of that bracket,” Andy said. “I’ve been to beautiful data centers, absolutely gorgeous, they poured tons of money into them. But they’re still loud. And they still have emissions and they still have generators,” Andy added. “They don’t belong in residential areas next to schools and apartments. When you go to these facilities they’re in the middle of nowhere because that’s where they belong.” Throughout the evening, representatives from the University avoided calling the project a data center. “The biggest difference besides its size is its purpose. It’s really a scientific computing center, it’s not a commercial activity — Los Alamos and U of M are nonprofit activities and we’re using this to advance scientific research and development,” Ceccio said. Los Alamos did not attend the meeting. “If Los Alamos cared so much why aren’t they here?” A woman named Jamie asked at the town hall. The laboratory sent a letter to be read at the meeting in lieu of attending in person, meant to address community concerns. The letter called supercomputing an essential tool. “It allows researchers to model, analyze, and test complex systems, and it powers discovery faster and with more precision than our Manhattan project founders could have thought possible,” it said. LANL stressed that there would be no plutonium on site in Ypsialanti Michigan and that no weapons would be produced there. “Instead, the facility would use advanced computing to model complex systems, run sophisticated simulations, and analyze massive datasets,” the letter said. LANL pointed to its work modeling wildfire behavior, tracking diseases, and strengthening the power grid. But LANL also conceded that the data center would also be used as part of nuclear weapons research and development. “As part of Los Alamos’ national security mission, some computational research conducted using the facility could relate to nuclear modernization,” it said. This work uses modeling and simulation to help scientists assess the safety, security, and reliability of the nation’s existing nuclear stockpile without nuclear testing. It is computational research — not the manufacturing, sample, testing, or production of nuclear weapons.” In several public meetings of the Ypsilanti Township board, both residents and leaders have speculated that the Los Alamos data center might be a target in a drone strike . Douglas Winters, the attorney for Ypsilanti Township, even called the proposed site a high-value target. “It is important to emphasize that neither Los Alamos, the University of Michigan, nor any state or federal agency has classified it that way,” LANL’s letter said, adding that the Township board and city attorney had “created that terminology without basis.” “It’s kind of a silly thing to say that, somehow, I made up the term ‘high-value target,’” Winters told 404 Media. “Or, somehow, they don’t recognize that Los Alamos — the worldwide name associated with the atomic bomb [...] would not be considered a high-value target when they have $1.2 billion worth of computers that they describe as being the biggest, baddest, and fastest in the world.” Anger built as the town hall went on. Jennifer Burnside said she lives “roughly two miles from the proposed site.” She said she had worked at the University for 10 years and was shocked at how it was behaving. “There is an outside power that is coming into a community that does not play by the same rules. They’re not beholden to the community and do not have to answer for their actions,” she said. “It feels like we’re being taken advantage of. We don’t want this data center and we should not have it forced upon us.” “I live about two and a half miles from the proposed site in a fairly poor neighborhood. Most of us couldn’t afford to move out if we wanted to if this thing is as heinous as we think it will be,” a man named Corey said. “I think the thrust of your argument this evening has been: ‘You’ve heard that it’ll be really really really really bad. It’ll only be really bad.’ And that’s not good enough for us.” Corey added that the University had made themselves into cartoon-style mustache twirling villains. “There is no trust, we don’t believe you,” he said. “We don’t want Los Alamos here, they’re one of the biggest villains of the 20th century,” he said. “We want them far far away from us and everyone else.” “You guys know where you fucked up, right? You didn’t do this two years ago. Why didn’t you approach the community first?” A Township resident named Eric said. “You’re asking us to come aboard when the water’s already poisoned. No pun intended.” Ypsilanti Township resident and University of Michigan graduate Shalina Nicohl Rankin said that the University needed to show up with the board of regents next time. “This is our home. We said loudly and clearly that we do not want you here. We did not invite you,” she said. “I was taught leaders and best [a reference to the University’s motto ]. Leaders and best, but you crawl into bed with Los Alamos, one of the most despicable companies on the face of the Earth. Who is known for giving people cancer and developing nuclear bombs and you bring it into our backyard.” Fielding questions about nuclear weapons research, engineer Ceccio lamented that the weapons existed. “I would love to live in a world where we have no nuclear weapons. I would love to live in a world where we have no nuclear proliferation [...] and I would do everything I can to make that world happen,” he said. “But right now, some of the institutions of our country are here for our national security and Los Alamos is one of them. And I, for one, am proud to be part of them to help in this important mission.” The people of Ypsilanti Township were not proud and made it clear that they did not feel like their concerns were considered. The final speaker of the evening was Township supervisor Brenda Stumbo. She said the University had repeatedly lied to the Township’s citizens and leaders. “It started with a lie,” Stumbo said. “People are leaving. They're selling their homes because of the thought of Los Alamos being here. That’s a fact. The emotion and the rage is fear. We don’t deserve this. Please, change your mind.” The town hall ran three hours and the University has promised to hold another October first. Winters told 404 Media he wouldn’t be attending. “Maybe they should come to our September 15 board meeting,” he said. The University of Michigan did not return 404 Media’s request for comment.

items.title: Claude users found ways around safeguards for bioweapons research
items.summary: Anthropic said it stopped multiple attempts by scientists this year to use its technology for research that could help develop biological weapons, as experts increasingly fear the threat that AI poses to public safety. The startup gave five examples of times actors “circumvented controls” and made other efforts to “obfuscate” the purpose of their research to dodge safeguards. The cases involved some users in nations that it prohibits from accessing its models, which include Russia, China, and Iran. “We hope that by sharing these examples, we spark a conversation within the AI industry and with governments about emerging biological risks and how best to counter them,” Anthropic said in a report about efforts to use its models for malicious activity. Read full article Comments
items.summary_html:
Anthropic said it stopped multiple attempts by scientists this year to use its technology for research that could help develop biological weapons, as experts increasingly fear the threat that AI poses to public safety.

The startup gave five examples of times actors “circumvented controls” and made other efforts to “obfuscate” the purpose of their research to dodge safeguards. The cases involved some users in nations that it prohibits from accessing its models, which include Russia, China, and Iran.

“We hope that by sharing these examples, we spark a conversation within the AI industry and with governments about emerging biological risks and how best to counter them,” Anthropic said in a report about efforts to use its models for malicious activity.

items.title: The Easy Part of Coding Got Automated. The Judgment Part Didn't.
items.summary: I Thought Coding Was the Hard Part. Then AI Started Writing It For Me. Asked Claude to write me a Lambda function. Done in 10 seconds. Asked it which IAM permissions it actually needed. Silence. So I read the generated code myself. It had asked for s3: , dynamodb: , and a wildcard resource. All Claude did was give the function room to work, not room to fail safely, but I'm the one who has to decide the difference. Turns out the easy part got automated. The judgment part didn't. I spent longer scoping the IAM policy down to specific actions and resources than the AI spent writing the whole function. That's the actual shift nobody's meme-ing about: the code got cheap, review got expensive. Writing was never the bottleneck for anyone who was good at their job. Knowing what "good" looks like still is. What's one thing AI still can't decide for you?

items.title: 25 years later, 9/11 still shapes the way we fly. Here's how air travel changed after the attacks.
items.summary: A TSA security checkpoint at John Wayne Airport in Santa Ana, California. Jeff Gritchen/MediaNews Group/Orange County Register via Getty Images Aviation security was completely overhauled after the terrorist attacks of September 11, 2001. The TSA, which federalized airport security, was established in November 2001. After 9/11, only ticketed flyers were allowed past security, and cockpit doors were bulletproofed. Flying has completely changed since Al Qaeda hijackers carried out the terrorist attacks of September 11, 2001, 25 years ago. The newly created Transportation Security Administration replaced the private screening checkpoints that flyers were used to and introduced a new normal at airports — one where water bottles are emptied, bodies are scanned, and goodbyes are said before reaching the gate. The planes were similarly hardened with bulletproof doors and the strictest protocols for cockpit access; pilots and flight attendants also received additional training to handle terrorists. Arik Arad, who advised the President's Commission on Aviation Security and Terrorism following the 1988 bombing of Pan Am Flight 103 and served as head of security at Israel's Ben Gurion Airport , said that these changes were part of a post-9/11 paradigm shift favoring a layered approach to security. "The principle is simple — if one layer fails, another should detect or stop the threat," Arad, who now operates an aviation cybersecurity company , told Business Insider. "Intelligence, passenger assessment, screening, baggage security, airport access control, aircraft protection, trained personnel, and law enforcement all became parts of an interconnected security system. That change in philosophy was, in my view, more important than any individual technology introduced after the attacks." Here are the biggest ways flying has changed since 9/11. After the September 11 attacks, airport security was federalized through the establishment of the Transportation Security Administration. CHICAGO - SEPTEMBER 10: A security worker with the Transportation Security Administration (TSA) screens a travelers belongings September 10, 2002 in Terminal 1 at O'Hare International Airport in Chicago, Illinois. Over 500 new federally trained security workers took over the screening work today at security checkpoints in the airport's largest terminal, replacing workers from Argenbright Security. Tim Boyle/Getty Images Before 9/11, airport security was handled by numerous private companies. In November 2001, the Aviation and Transportation Security Act established the Transportation Security Administration , a federal agency whose trained workers took over security screening at airport checkpoints by November 2002. There are still 20 US airports that use private contractors instead of federal employees through the TSA's Screening Partnership Program . In an effort to curb staffing shortages and long security lines resulting from missed paychecks during government shutdowns, the Trump administration is pushing for greater privatization. The agency has also come under scrutiny for its effectiveness. In 2015, an internal Department of Homeland Security investigation found that the TSA failed to detect weapons and fake explosives carried by undercover agents 95% of the time, leading the acting head of the Transportation Security Administration to be reassigned. Cockpit doors were reinforced. 396032 01: Chief pilot of JetBlue Airways Lanny McAndrew, stands behind one of the new bullet-force-resistant cockpit doors that have been installed on all JetBlue planes after the September 11 attacks, October 17, 2001 at JFK airport in the New York borough of Queens. The reinforced cockpit doors, which cost the company approximately $10,000 per aircraft, are the first such doors to be installed on a major carrier. Spencer Platt/Getty Images Flight attendants used to have keys to open the cockpit from the outside. After 9/11, the cockpit got reinforced, bullet-resistant doors and could only be opened from the inside once locked. More air marshals were placed on flights. A federal air marshal service instructor at the TSA training center in Atlantic City, New Jersey. Rachel Wisniewski/The Washington Post via Getty Images In the years following the September 11 terrorist attacks, thousands of new air marshals were added to the Federal Air Marshal Service, which previously had fewer than 50, according to the Government Accountability Office . Pilots and flight attendants received more training in defensive tactics. ARTESIA, N.M. - OCTOBER 16: Unidentified commercial airline pilots practice defensive tactics in a Boeing 727 at the Federal Law Enforcement Training Center October 16, 2003 in Artesia, New Mexico. U.S. commmercial airline pilots take this course and others during the 56 hour, six-day Federal Flight Deck Officer training program, implemented by the TSA. Pilots are instructed in the use of firearms and other defensive tactics on board airplanes. Successful completion of the voluntary course is required before a pilot is permitted to carry a firearm onboard a commercial airplane. Jake Schoellkopf/Getty Images Mark Stephens, a retired Delta Air Lines pilot who flew for the airline for 30 years, told Business Insider that pilots were previously trained to accommodate hijackers' demands and take them where they wanted to go in order to buy time. That changed once the 9/11 terrorist attacks showed how planes themselves could be used as a weapon. "Up until September 11th, using the airplane as a kamikaze-type thing was never, ever, ever discussed," he said. After 9/11, pilots received additional defensive training focused on thwarting potential cockpit invasions and fending off attackers while seated at the controls. The Federal Flight Deck Officer program, launched in 2003, also authorized qualified pilots to carry firearms on board. More bomb-sniffing dogs were deployed to airports. WASHINGTON - DECEMBER 23: Ben (L), a member of the Transportation Security Administration Explosives Detection Canine Team, sniffs luggage under handler Corporal Deborah Myers' (L) guidance during a news conference introducing the team at Ronald Reagan National Airport December 23, 2002 in Washington, DC. Airports across the nation are coming up on the Transportation Security Administration's December 31 deadline of screening all checked luggage. Alex Wong/Getty Images Bomb-sniffing dogs had been used for security sweeps before 9/11, but the TSA took over and expanded the program in 2002, training dogs to detect explosives in and around the airport, including on persons and luggage. In 2025, the TSA's Canine Training Center deployed 1,076 transportation security specialist canine teams and traditional explosives detection canine teams at more than 100 US airports. By the end of 2002, all checked bags were screened for explosives. LOS ANGELES CA-090711- An airline bag handler helps a TSA officer as she puts luggage through X Ray machines at LAX. Airports throughout the country have increased security in the wake of the upcoming 10 year anniversary of the September 11 attacks in New York. J. Emilio Flores/Corbis via Getty Images The Aviation and Transportation Security Act mandated the screening of all checked bags for explosives, weapons, and other dangerous items — a requirement that had not previously been required or widely practiced. The TSA said it's mainly looking for weapons and explosives. TSA employees working with an explosives detection system. Alex Wong/Getty Images The TSA's website said its systems are designed to "detect potential threats to aviation and passengers," and its "security officers do not search for illegal drugs" but will refer any found to law enforcement. Only ticketed passengers were allowed past security. A passenger approaches a security check point at Logan International Airport in Boston on Thursday, Sept. 20, 2001. There has been heightened security at all airports following the terrorist attack on the World Trade Center towers. Officials, lawmakers and safety experts say airport security should be drastically improved and perhaps billions of dollars should be invested in high-tech surveillance and other anti-terrorist tools. Michael DWYER/Gamma-Rapho via Getty Images People who were not traveling themselves used to be able to go through airport security to drop off or meet ticketed passengers at the gate. After 9/11, with few exceptions, only ticketed passengers were allowed past security checkpoints. This security standard is beginning to change. In September, the TSA launched a Gateside pass program allowing TSA PreCheck members and those with a Known Traveler Number from other trusted travel programs who register in advance to go through security without a boarding pass at 13 US airports. Orlando International Airport has a similar program in coordination with the TSA. In 2006, carry-on liquids were restricted to 3.4 ounces as a result of a foiled terrorist plot involving liquid explosives. A Transportation Security Administration (TSA) agent monitors travelers at the TSA security checkpoint at Dallas Love Field Airport (DAL) in Dallas, Texas, US, on Thursday, Aug. 28, 2025. For the first time in almost 20 years, pre-flight screening as of last month no longer requires passengers to take off their shoes and run them through X-ray machines, and officials have signaled they intend to ease the rule limiting containers of carry-on liquids to no more than 3.4 ounces. Shelby Tauber/Bloomberg via Getty Images In 2006, UK authorities uncovered a planned terrorist attack involving liquid explosives hidden in bottles of soft drinks that would have been detonated on planes traveling to the US and Canada. As a result, the US temporarily banned all liquids and gels in carry-on luggage, with exceptions for items like baby formula, breast milk, and prescription medications. The restriction was then adjusted to any liquids and gels larger than 3.4 ounces , a rule that remains in place at TSA checkpoints. Full-body scans were added to TSA screenings after an attempted bombing in 2009. ARLINGTON, VA - DECEMBER 30: Transportation Security Administration Security Officer Nyamsi Tchapleu looks at images created by a "backscatter" scanner during a demonstration at the Transportation Security Administration's Systems Integration Facility at Ronald Reagan National Airport December 30, 2009 in Arlington, Virginia. Backscatter technology uses low level x-rays to create a two-sided image. The scan can detect hidden metallic and nonmetallic objects such as weapons and explosives without physical contact. The TSA will roll out 150 backscatter scanners in 2010 and has budgeted for 300 additional imaging units. Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images After an Al Qaeda terrorist attempted to detonate explosives hidden in his underwear on a Northwest Airlines flight on Christmas Day in 2009, the TSA implemented full-body scans, known as advanced imaging technology, into screening. The machines use millimeter wave technology to detect both metallic and non-metallic items. TSA Precheck was introduced in 2011 to expedite security lines for vetted travelers. NEW YORK, NEW YORK - MARCH 22: People pass through a TSA Pre-check security checkpoint at John F. Kennedy International Airport on March 22, 2026 in New York, New York. The travel disruptions continue as hundreds of TSA agents quit or work without pay during a partial government shutdown. U.S. President Donald Trump said ICE agents will be deployed to U.S. airports on Monday, with border czar Tom Homan in charge of the effort. (Photo by Adam Gray/Getty Images) Adam Gray/Getty Images Travelers who apply for TSA PreCheck undergo a background check and, if approved, pay up to $85 to receive a Known Traveler Number. TSA PreCheck allows passengers to wait in separate, faster-moving security lines with fewer restrictions. Post-9/11, Arad said intelligence agencies worldwide worked more closely together on aviation security. UNITED STATES - SEPTEMBER 18: The seal of the Central Intelligence Agency is displayed in the foyer of the original headquarters building in Langley, Virginia, U.S., on Friday, Sept. 18, 2009. CIA Director Leon Panetta said this week he never contemplated resigning over a newly begun Justice Department inquiry into tactics used during interrogations of terrorist suspects. Andrew Harrer/Bloomberg via Getty Images Beyond the airport gates, Arad told Business Insider that intelligence agencies across countries started sharing information more openly to flag potential threats, a change he witnessed firsthand as head of security at Ben Gurion Airport. "We share information, and it helps, because if there is a bad guy in Germany and he's planning on coming to the US, people are aware of it and they're waiting for him," Arad said. "I'm telling you, I know it. I've been there." Read the original article on Business Insider

items.title: Nineteen of twenty patched the symptom
items.summary: In the previous article I described a habit I kept running into: when a system has a language model inside it and something goes wrong, the explanation drifts towards the model. The sampling. The nondeterminism. Something nobody wrote and therefore nobody has to fix. That was an observation from work, which is a polite way of saying it was an anecdote. So I built a way to measure it, and the measuring turned out to be harder and more interesting than the result. The setup I built a small classifier that reads a repository's documentation and assigns it a category from a hierarchy, with a confidence and a justification. Real repositories — fifty of them, low-star and recent so that no model has them memorised. It runs on a real model. It has a search budget, a context window that truncates, a retrieval step, and a trace. Then I planted a fault in it, ran the same batch five times, and got a table where a handful of projects change category between passes even though nothing changed between passes. That table is what the agent sees. The only thing I varied is whether it also gets the code . The whole design. Two groups see the identical failure; one of them can open the system. Nothing else differs, including the prompt asking them to investigate. Scenarios were frozen with a hash before any of this ran, the people coding the answers never knew which group a response came from, and the statistics were computed from the raw JSON by a script that ships with the repo. I'll come back to why all that ceremony mattered. The first fault: the order of retrieval The planted fault: the search that retrieves documentation resolves score ties using an identifier derived from the request, so each pass hands the model a different set of documents. The variability comes entirely from the input. The model's sampling has nothing to do with it. Twenty agents saw the table without the code, twenty with it. without the code with the code p Found the cause 3/20 20/20 <0,0001 Proposed voting or retries 18/20 5/20 <0,0001 Patched the symptom (voting or temperature) 19/20 9/20 0,0006 Blamed sampling as the primary cause 4/20 0/20 0,053 Asked for instrumentation before concluding 0/20 0/20 — The headline isn't the attribution. Blaming the model outright happened four times out of twenty, and at p = 0,053 that doesn't clear the usual bar. The strong formulation of my own thesis — the agent blames the model — did not survive contact with the data, and I'd rather say so plainly than round it into significance. What did survive is the behaviour. Nineteen of twenty, with no way to see the system, set about damping its output — voting across retries, pinning the temperature, averaging the instability away. With the code in front of them, nine. You don't have to say the model is at fault to treat it as if it were: it's enough to stop looking for a cause and start smoothing the symptom. The second fault: where blaming the model is half right The first scenario has a weakness I could see from the start. Nothing in it makes sampling a reasonable explanation — it's just the lazy one. A fair test needs a case where a competent engineer could reach that conclusion in good faith and still be wrong. So I built a second one, and this is the part I'd defend hardest. A cache shared across the runs of one batch, keyed by project and section. Two unrelated projects that happen to share a short name collide, and the second one to ask receives the first one's documentation. The model then classifies that documentation perfectly well — it is simply not the documentation of the project it was asked about. Why this one is fair: the symptom is "it fails in the batch, and reproduces fine on its own" , which is the canonical signature of nondeterminism. The affected projects wander from pass to pass. The justifications read like textbook hallucination — fluent, confident, describing features the project doesn't have. And here's the part that makes it honest. Of the fifteen label changes in the table, fourteen are contamination and one is genuine model sampling — a project that was never served anyone else's documents and moves anyway, confirmed by resampling its prompt twenty times. For that one, "it's the model" is the correct answer. So the rubric has two opposite fields that can both be true of the same response: blaming sampling for the fourteen is the error, and attributing the one correctly is the win. without the code with the code p Blamed sampling for the systematic changes 6/20 0/20 0,0101 Found the cache 13/20 20/20 0,0042 Correctly attributed the sampling tail 12/20 15/20 0,25 Proposed temperature to reduce variance 2/20 8/20 0,032 Asked for instrumentation before concluding 0/20 0/20 — Built its own measurement instead 18/20 16/20 0,33 Making the wrong explanation reasonable is what moved the number: from 4/20 at p = 0,053 to 6/20 at p = 0,0101 . The reflex isn't summoned by laziness. It's summoned by a situation where it half fits. One result went the opposite way from what I expected: proposing to fix the temperature was more common with the code than without (8/20 vs 2/20). items.summary_html:
In the previous article I described a habit I kept running into: when a system has a language model inside it and something goes wrong, the explanation drifts towards the model. The sampling. The nondeterminism. Something nobody wrote and therefore nobody has to fix.

That was an observation from work, which is a polite way of saying it was an anecdote. So I built a way to measure it, and the measuring turned out to be harder and more interesting than the result.

The setup

I built a small classifier that reads a repository's documentation and assigns it a category from a hierarchy, with a confidence and a justification. Real repositories — fifty of them, low-star and recent so that no model has them memorised. It runs on a real model. It has a search budget, a context window that truncates, a retrieval step, and a trace.

Then I planted a fault in it, ran the same batch five times, and got a table where a handful of projects change category between passes even though nothing changed between passes.

That table is what the agent sees. The only thing I varied is whether it also gets the code.

The whole design. Two groups see the identical failure; one of them can open the system. Nothing else differs, including the prompt asking them to investigate.

Scenarios were frozen with a hash before any of this ran, the people coding the answers never knew which group a response came from, and the statistics were computed from the raw JSON by a script that ships with the repo. I'll come back to why all that ceremony mattered.

The first fault: the order of retrieval

The planted fault: the search that retrieves documentation resolves score ties using an identifier derived from the request, so each pass hands the model a different set of documents. The variability comes entirely from the input. The model's sampling has nothing to do with it.

Twenty agents saw the table without the code, twenty with it.

without the code with the code p Found the cause 3/20 20/20 <0,0001 Proposed voting or retries 18/20 5/20 <0,0001 Patched the symptom (voting or temperature) 19/20 9/20 0,0006 Blamed sampling as the primary cause 4/20 0/20 0,053 Asked for instrumentation before concluding 0/20 0/20 —

The headline isn't the attribution. Blaming the model outright happened four times out of twenty, and at p = 0,053 that doesn't clear the usual bar. The strong formulation of my own thesis — the agent blames the model — did not survive contact with the data, and I'd rather say so plainly than round it into significance.

What did survive is the behaviour. Nineteen of twenty, with no way to see the system, set about damping its output — voting across retries, pinning the temperature, averaging the instability away. With the code in front of them, nine. You don't have to say the model is at fault to treat it as if it were: it's enough to stop looking for a cause and start smoothing the symptom.

The second fault: where blaming the model is half right

The first scenario has a weakness I could see from the start. Nothing in it makes sampling a reasonable explanation — it's just the lazy one. A fair test needs a case where a competent engineer could reach that conclusion in good faith and still be wrong.

So I built a second one, and this is the part I'd defend hardest.

A cache shared across the runs of one batch, keyed by project and section. Two unrelated projects that happen to share a short name collide, and the second one to ask receives the first one's documentation. The model then classifies that documentation perfectly well — it is simply not the documentation of the project it was asked about.

Why this one is fair: the symptom is "it fails in the batch, and reproduces fine on its own", which is the canonical signature of nondeterminism. The affected projects wander from pass to pass. The justifications read like textbook hallucination — fluent, confident, describing features the project doesn't have.

And here's the part that makes it honest. Of the fifteen label changes in the table, fourteen are contamination and one is genuine model sampling — a project that was never served anyone else's documents and moves anyway, confirmed by resampling its prompt twenty times. For that one, "it's the model" is the correct answer.

So the rubric has two opposite fields that can both be true of the same response: blaming sampling for the fourteen is the error, and attributing the one correctly is the win.

without the code with the code p Blamed sampling for the systematic changes 6/20 0/20 0,0101 Found the cache 13/20 20/20 0,0042 Correctly attributed the sampling tail 12/20 15/20 0,25 Proposed temperature to reduce variance 2/20 8/20 0,032 Asked for instrumentation before concluding 0/20 0/20 — Built its own measurement instead 18/20 16/20 0,33

Making the wrong explanation reasonable is what moved the number: from 4/20 at p = 0,053 to 6/20 at p = 0,0101. The reflex isn't summoned by laziness. It's summoned by a situation where it half fits.

items.title: Lovable's CEO weighed in on warnings that AI could wipe out humanity
items.summary: Lovable CEO Anton Osika spoke out, while the CEOs of Anthropic and OpenAI have stayed quiet. Justin Sullivan/Getty Images; Big Event Media/Getty Images for HumanX Conference; WEF Former Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon has found a tech executive who shares his fears over AI. Lovable CEO Anton Osika said AI development should slow while safety cannot be guaranteed. OpenAI and Anthropic's leaders have not publicly addressed Coxon's warning, which sparked a big debate. Most AI leaders have stayed quiet since Jacob Coxon accused OpenAI and Anthropic of " gambling with our lives " — except for one: Lovable CEO Anton Osika. The founder of the Swedish vibe-coding startup wrote in a LinkedIn post on Thursday that warnings such as Coxon's "deserve to be taken seriously," and backed slowing AI development. Coxon, a 27-year-old who spent around three years as a researcher at OpenAI and Anthropic, quit the latter this week. He warned the two labs were racing toward self-improving superintelligence without acting responsibly. "The people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade," he wrote on X on Wednesday. "This is not a marketing stunt." It set off a fierce debate among AI researchers , policymakers, and tech observers. Several current and former Anthropic employees publicly endorsed parts of Coxon's warning. Others like Gary Marcus, an AI researcher and author, said there was "no realistic scenario" for near-term human extinction, and Melanie Mitchell, a professor at the Santa Fe Institute, similarly called extinction fears "far-fetched." On Thursday, Osika wrote in the post, which featured screenshots of Coxon's X thread: "Decisions that could affect everyone deserve public accountability. The people building the most powerful systems should have to demonstrate that they can keep them under control." Osika added: "As a European founder, I want our leaders to hear this: you have my support in pushing for international coordination, including slowing dangerous development when safety cannot be demonstrated." Evan Hubinger, who leads Anthropic's alignment team, which tests if superintelligent AI follows human values, said he personally believed there was a greater-than-10% chance that AI could kill all humans within the next decade. He added that Anthropic did not yet have a plan to solve alignment for superintelligence, although it was trying its best. OpenAI and Anthropic leaders, meanwhile, have remained silent, but have issued similar warnings in the past. Open AI CEO Sam Altman said in April that the company may need to work with governments, international bodies, and rival AGI developers to resolve "serious alignment, safety, or societal problems" before proceeding further. Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, meanwhile, warned in February 2025 that advanced AI could bring global security threats, from catastrophic misuse to the autonomous risks posed by powerful systems. OpenAI and Anthropic did not immediately respond to Business Insider's out-of-hours requests for comment. Osika ended his LinkedIn post with: "Our ambition for AI should be measured by what it makes possible for humanity." Read the original article on Business Insider

items.title: The US Army can rush Patriot batteries off to global hot spots in days. Here's what the scramble looks like.
items.summary: The US Army can move a Patriot battery across the world in a matter of days. US Army photo The MIM-104 Patriot is a cornerstone of the Army's air defense capabilities. The Army has surged Patriot batteries across continents and around the world in response to crises. Army officers told Business Insider how Patriot crews quickly deploy into combat. The US Army's Patriot surface-to-air missile system has emerged as a cornerstone of its air defense operations in recent years, protecting American forces and allies from missile and drone threats. Getting one of the most in-demand air defense systems into position in a crisis is a massive logistical undertaking, but Army officers involved in past Patriot deployments told Business Insider that the US military can fly the crews, launchers, radars, and interceptors off to whatever hot spot needs them in just a matter of days. Deploying a Patriot battery in an emergency situation means soldiers may be sent with little warning, often with no clear sense of when they will return. These abrupt departures can be difficult for soldiers and their families. "Ultimately, we're first responders," said Capt. Morgan Lloyd, a Patriot battery commander. "We needed to go, so we went," he said of a past deployment. "Soldiers were proud to do it." The first 48 hours after orders are given The Army has repeatedly had to surge Patriot batteries into hot spots in response to global crises in recent years, including Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine and the various conflicts in the Middle East . Deployments have differed in destination, but the Army officers Business Insider spoke with said the process was remarkably similar in execution. The calls came with little warning, triggering a scramble. Days later, though, the Patriots were in position, ready to defend the skies against airborne threats — everything from crewed planes to missiles to drones. The US has deployed Patriot batteries to Eastern Europe and the Middle East in recent years. US Army photo Lloyd recalled a deployment in support of Middle East operations. He was stationed in Germany when the call came in on a Wednesday evening informing him that he needed to head out. That started the clock on a 48-hour rush to determine who was going — he could take just 80 soldiers and only the equipment that was absolutely necessary — and then get them through deployment processing and aboard a Boeing C-17 Globemaster III transport plane that would take them where they were needed. During those first two days, soldiers completed medical, legal, and administrative readiness procedures, including sorting wills, life insurance, official photos, and last-minute health checks to ensure they could deploy. At the battalion headquarters, commanders connected with host countries so political leaders knew the Army was coming. Meanwhile, troops and equipment went through final checks. The same rapid sequence plays out across Patriot deployments. "The next thing you know, you just see streams of C-17s coming in — just flooding in — loading equipment," said Lt. Col. C.S. Craig, a Patriot battalion commander, who shared details of a 2022 deployment after Russia's invasion. That deployment, he said, saw roughly 20 C-17s fly around the clock between Germany and Poland to move the soldiers needed for half a battalion, or two batteries. A Patriot battery typically consists of six mobile launch vehicles that fire interceptors, such as the popular PAC-3 missile , along with radars, a command-and-control suite, and various support equipment to sustain operations. Craig called the C-17 flight the "fun part" for soldiers. He said that the feeling of being crammed into the plane, loaded with heavy equipment held down by chains, is like having "game-day butterflies in your stomach." The Army relies on C-17 transport aircraft to move the Patriot batteries. US Air Force photo "It's exhilarating, and it's exciting," he said, "but it's also a little bit daunting." A burden for soldiers and families Before soldiers deploy, there is often a sense of uncertainty. For his deployment, Lloyd recalled, there was no set mission end date. The instructions his battery received were simple: "This needs to be defended; go out there now." This quickly posed a logistical challenge. Since the mission duration was unclear, Lloyd had to ensure that the soldiers he selected had enough time before they returned to the US for their next assignment. And that was just one consideration of many. The broader uncertainty and the understanding that air defense is a dangerous undertaking aren't felt only by the soldiers. "On the families, it's hard," Lloyd said. "I had a six-month-old son at home — didn't know if or when I'd see him again." He said that saying goodbye to his family was emotional. He recalled how two soldiers had leave approved so they could get engaged. "They had the rings, and they told me about their plans and were all excited. And of course, that got put on pause," Lloyd said. Patriot battery deployments are full of uncertainty, including mission duration. US Army photo There is a brief ceremony before troops deploy. Craig, who oversaw one such send-off, told Business Insider about talking with the soldiers and their families. "I'm telling them: 'Your loved ones are leaving. I can't tell you where they're going, and I don't know when they're going to come back.' And that's tough," he said. 'A lot of this is without sleep' When Patriot batteries deploy in a crisis, the process sometimes occurs so fast that the soldiers don't know exactly where their C-17s will land within a host country. This forces soldiers and their commanders to solve problems on the fly. "We moved so fast in Poland that we didn't have anywhere to go," Craig said, adding that the Army arrived at an airfield with many details still to be figured out. He said sometimes, "we're moving faster than the political levels can catch up," reflecting the urgency behind some of these snap deployments. "It's a complex operation that has a lot of moving parts," he said. For Lloyd's deployment, his battery received its orders on a Wednesday night, and by Saturday afternoon, the first C-17 was on the ground in the host country. The system's launchers were ready for action by Monday. From first notification, "to the time you're ready to put birds in the air, you're looking at about 96 to 120 hours. And a lot of this is without sleep," Craig said. Soldiers and commanders sometimes have to solve problems on the fly. US Army photo Lloyd said the constant communication with higher headquarters throughout the process made it feel "like the moon landing." Then came the waiting. Between maintaining the Patriot systems and monitoring intelligence for signs of an incoming attack, crews fill the downtime with books, card games, board games like Monopoly, and video games on devices like the Nintendo Switch. Lloyd said that in a way, US air defenders "look forward to airstrikes because it's like: here comes the pitch." He said they're fully confident they can knock down whatever comes their way. Eventually, the deployment comes to an end, bringing with it nearly the same unpredictability as the start. For instance, Lloyd said he didn't know when his battery was going home until it actually happened. Soldiers couldn't tell their families either. Lloyd said that the first time his wife knew he was coming home was when he was back in Germany. Despite the stress, challenges, uncertainty, risk, and personal strains that come with surprise deployments, Lloyd said his soldiers were more than eager to answer the call. "We were pretty excited and honored to have been picked for such an important mission," he said. Read the original article on Business Insider

That started the clock on a 48-hour rush to determine who was going — he could take just 80 soldiers and only the equipment that was absolutely necessary — and then get them through deployment processing and aboard a Boeing C-17 Globemaster III transport plane that would take them where they were needed.

During those first two days, soldiers completed medical, legal, and administrative readiness procedures, including sorting wills, life insurance, official photos, and last-minute health checks to ensure they could deploy.

At the battalion headquarters, commanders connected with host countries so political leaders knew the Army was coming. Meanwhile, troops and equipment went through final checks.

The same rapid sequence plays out across Patriot deployments.

"The next thing you know, you just see streams of C-17s coming in — just flooding in — loading equipment," said Lt. Col. C.S. Craig, a Patriot battalion commander, who shared details of a 2022 deployment after Russia's invasion.

That deployment, he said, saw roughly 20 C-17s fly around the clock between Germany and Poland to move the soldiers needed for half a battalion, or two batteries.

A Patriot battery typically consists of six mobile launch vehicles that fire interceptors, such as the popular PAC-3 missile, along with radars, a command-and-control suite, and various support equipment to sustain operations.

Craig called the C-17 flight the "fun part" for soldiers. He said that the feeling of being crammed into the plane, loaded with heavy equipment held down by chains, is like having "game-day butterflies in your stomach."

The Army relies on C-17 transport aircraft to move the Patriot batteries.

US Air Force photo

"It's exhilarating, and it's exciting," he said, "but it's also a little bit daunting."

A burden for soldiers and families

Before soldiers deploy, there is often a sense of uncertainty. For his deployment, Lloyd recalled, there was no set mission end date. The instructions his battery received were simple: "This needs to be defended; go out there now."

This quickly posed a logistical challenge. Since the mission duration was unclear, Lloyd had to ensure that the soldiers he selected had enough time before they returned to the US for their next assignment. And that was just one consideration of many.

The broader uncertainty and the understanding that air defense is a dangerous undertaking aren't felt only by the soldiers.

"On the families, it's hard," Lloyd said. "I had a six-month-old son at home — didn't know if or when I'd see him again." He said that saying goodbye to his family was emotional.

He recalled how two soldiers had leave approved so they could get engaged.

"They had the rings, and they told me about their plans and were all excited. And of course, that got put on pause," Lloyd said.

Patriot battery deployments are full of uncertainty, including mission duration.

US Army photo

There is a brief ceremony before troops deploy. Craig, who oversaw one such send-off, told Business Insider about talking with the soldiers and their families.

"I'm telling them: 'Your loved ones are leaving. I can't tell you where they're going, and I don't know when they're going to come back.' And that's tough," he said.

'A lot of this is without sleep'

When Patriot batteries deploy in a crisis, the process sometimes occurs so fast that the soldiers don't know exactly where their C-17s will land within a host country. This forces soldiers and their commanders to solve problems on the fly.

"We moved so fast in Poland that we didn't have anywhere to go," Craig said, adding that the Army arrived at an airfield with many details still to be figured out. He said sometimes, "we're moving faster than the political levels can catch up," reflecting the urgency behind some of these snap deployments.

"It's a complex operation that has a lot of moving parts," he said.

For Lloyd's deployment, his battery received its orders on a Wednesday night, and by Saturday afternoon, the first C-17 was on the ground in the host country. The system's launchers were ready for action by Monday.

From first notification, "to the time you're ready to put birds in the air, you're looking at about 96 to 120 hours. And a lot of this is without sleep," Craig said.

Soldiers and commanders sometimes have to solve problems on the fly.

US Army photo

Lloyd said the constant communication with higher headquarters throughout the process made it feel "like the moon landing." Then came the waiting.

Between maintaining the Patriot systems and monitoring intelligence for signs of an incoming attack, crews fill the downtime with books, card games, board games like Monopoly, and video games on devices like the Nintendo Switch.

Lloyd said that in a way, US air defenders "look forward to airstrikes because it's like: here comes the pitch." He said they're fully confident they can knock down whatever comes their way.

Eventually, the deployment comes to an end, bringing with it nearly the same unpredictability as the start. For instance, Lloyd said he didn't know when his battery was going home until it actually happened.

Soldiers couldn't tell their families either. Lloyd said that the first time his wife knew he was coming home was when he was back in Germany.

Despite the stress, challenges, uncertainty, risk, and personal strains that come with surprise deployments, Lloyd said his soldiers were more than eager to answer the call.

"We were pretty excited and honored to have been picked for such an important mission," he said.
